note: Batch B of AI-authored, source-grounded MCQs for the public-policy curriculum's data storytelling, leadership, professional communication, ethics & integrity, decision making, and change management competencies, grounded in the NITI Aayog National Data and Analytics Platform vision document, the Karmayogi Quality Framework, the PIB Mission Karmayogi cabinet announcement, the DARPG Sevottam citizen's charter guidelines, the CCS (Conduct) Rules 1964, the CBC MDO performance-measurement handbook, and UPSC CSP 2023 GS1.

questions.locator: Vision Document, statement of NDAP's Vision
questions.source_excerpt: Vision: Democratize access to public Government data through a world-class user experience.
questions.question: The NDAP Vision Document states a one-line 'Vision' for the platform, distinct from its Mission statement. What is that Vision?
options: Democratize access to public Government data through a world-class user experience
Standardize data across multiple Government sources for research and policy making
Centralize all Government IT infrastructure under a single national data centre
Replace all existing departmental dashboards with one unified reporting tool
questions.explanation: The Vision Document states the Vision verbatim as democratizing access to public Government data through a world-class user experience. The second option is actually NDAP's Mission statement, not its Vision, and the other two describe infrastructure-consolidation goals the document never states.

questions.locator: Vision Document, statement of NDAP's Mission
questions.source_excerpt: Mission: Standardize data across multiple Government sources, provide flexible analytics and make it easily accessible in formats conducive for research, innovation, policy making and public consumption.
questions.question: According to the Vision Document, which statement correctly captures NDAP's Mission (as opposed to its Vision)?
options: Democratize access to public Government data through a world-class user experience
Standardize data across multiple Government sources, provide flexible analytics, and make it easily accessible for research, innovation, policy making and public consumption
Enforce a single mandatory data format on every Ministry and Department
Award grants to private startups that build analytics tools on Government data
questions.explanation: The Mission statement in the Vision Document is to standardize data across sources, provide flexible analytics, and make it accessible in formats useful for research, innovation, policy making and public consumption. The first option is the Vision, not the Mission, and the other two are not stated anywhere in the document.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Objectives' panel (User-centric / Coherent / Up-to-date)
questions.source_excerpt: User-centric: Data access is user-friendly and engaging, tailored to the needs of policymakers, bureaucrats, researchers, innovators, data scientists, journalists and citizens alike. Coherent: Multiple data sets are presented using a standardized schema, by using common geographical and temporal identifiers. Up-to-date: Standard Operating Procedures are set to ensure data is updated regularly.
questions.question: The Vision Document organizes NDAP's objectives around three qualities of data access. Which set of three correctly names them?
options: Secure, Anonymized, Auditable
User-centric, Coherent, Up-to-date
Free, Open-source, Crowd-sourced
Real-time, Encrypted, Multilingual
questions.explanation: The document names three objectives: data access should be User-centric (tailored to different user groups), Coherent (a standardized schema with common geographic and temporal identifiers), and Up-to-date (kept current through SOPs). The other option sets are plausible-sounding but not the three terms the document actually uses.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Data Sources' panel
questions.source_excerpt: Websites of over 50 Ministries and Departments of the Central Government and data.gov.in. Websites of all Departments and Ministries of the State Government, not exceeding 250.
questions.question: As described in the Vision Document's 'Data Sources' section, roughly how broad is the intended scope of data feeding into NDAP?
options: Only data.gov.in and nothing else
A single pilot Ministry, to be expanded only after a multi-year trial
Over 50 Central Ministries/Departments plus data.gov.in, and up to 250 State Government Department/Ministry websites
Only private-sector data partnerships, since Government data was judged too inconsistent to use
questions.explanation: The Vision Document lists data sources as websites of over 50 Central Ministries and Departments plus data.gov.in, and websites of State Government Departments and Ministries not exceeding 250 -- a genuinely pan-India, multi-source scope from the outset, not a narrow pilot or a private-data-only approach.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Challenges' -- data not published in a user-centric manner
questions.source_excerpt: Data is not published in a user-centric manner. The current data formats are often not conducive for research and innovation... some datasets are only available in PDF, webpage or as an image, making it difficult for further analysis.
questions.question: The Vision Document identifies a specific challenge with how Indian Government data is currently published. What is it?
options: Most datasets are published only in PDF, webpage, or image form, which is difficult to analyse further even when dashboards with visualisations already exist
Government departments refuse to publish any data at all, even in dashboards
All datasets are already machine-readable, but citizens lack the technical skill to use them
Data is published promptly but only in encrypted formats inaccessible to the public
questions.explanation: The document notes that while many departments maintain dashboards with visualisations and downloadable options, some datasets remain locked in PDF, webpage or image form, which is hard to use for further research or analysis -- the opposite of the second and fourth options, and a different problem from the third, which assumes clean machine-readable data already exists.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Challenges' -- data ecosystem incoherence
questions.source_excerpt: Data ecosystem is incoherent due to different standards. Ministries and Departments do not use a shared standard for common indicators. Attributes like region and time period defined differently... a District Magistrate can access data across all departments for their district, easily, in one platform.
questions.question: The Vision Document uses the example of a District Magistrate needing data 'across all departments for their district, easily, in one platform' to illustrate which specific problem NDAP is meant to solve?
options: The shortage of trained data scientists in district administration
The lack of internet connectivity in rural districts
The incoherence caused by different Ministries/Departments defining common attributes like region and time period differently, which prevents datasets from 'speaking to each other'
The absence of any digitised government data whatsoever
questions.explanation: The District Magistrate example is used specifically to illustrate the coherence problem: because different Ministries and Departments define shared attributes such as region and time period inconsistently, a single official cannot easily combine their data -- it is not primarily a staffing, connectivity, or digitisation problem.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Approach'
questions.source_excerpt: We intend to draw inspiration from the best platforms around the world... as can be seen in platforms such as 'datausa.io' and 'data.gov.sg'.
questions.question: The Vision Document names two international platforms that inspired NDAP's approach to user experience. Which pair is it?
options: Google Trends and Kaggle
datausa.io and data.gov.sg
OECD.Stat and Eurostat
World Bank Open Data and IMF DataMapper
questions.explanation: The Vision Document explicitly names datausa.io and data.gov.sg as platforms whose seamless, interactive user experience NDAP wants to emulate. The other pairs are real international data platforms but are not the ones named in this document.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Approach' -- building on existing Indian platforms
questions.source_excerpt: Over the years, notable improvements have taken place in the data publishing ecosystem. For example, data.gov.in provides ready access to data from 165 departments. DISHA, by the Ministry of Rural Development, provides access to data from 42 schemes across 20 ministries.
questions.question: Besides drawing on international examples, the Vision Document says NDAP will build on the success of two existing Indian data platforms. Which two does it name, along with their approximate scope?
options: Aadhaar and DigiLocker
GeM (Government e-Marketplace) and UMANG
data.gov.in (165 departments) and DISHA (42 schemes across 20 ministries, Ministry of Rural Development)
MyGov and PM-Kisan portal
questions.explanation: The document names data.gov.in, which already provides data from 165 departments, and DISHA, run by the Ministry of Rural Development, giving access to data from 42 schemes across 20 ministries, as the two existing Indian platforms NDAP is meant to build on. The other options are real e-governance platforms but serve different purposes and are not mentioned in this document.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Approach' -- common schema across sectors
questions.source_excerpt: NDAP will provide access to data from multiple sectors in one place... This will be presented using a common schema, with clear definitions and narratives to help the user navigate the differences between similar data from different sources.
questions.question: A researcher wants to compare 'literacy rate' figures published separately by the Ministries of Education, Rural Development, and Statistics, each of which defines the indicator slightly differently. Which NDAP design feature is meant to directly address this situation?
options: A social-media share button attached to each dataset
A common schema across sectors, with clear definitions and narratives explaining differences between similar indicators from different sources
A rule restricting the platform to a single ministry's data at a time
A requirement that all users register with a government email address before viewing any data
questions.explanation: NDAP's common-schema feature, with explanatory narratives, is designed exactly for this cross-source comparability problem: it helps a user understand and reconcile differences between similarly-named indicators from different Ministries. A share button, a single-ministry restriction, or a login requirement do nothing to resolve definitional inconsistency.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Features'
questions.source_excerpt: Features: Facilitate analysis in R, Tableau, SAS. Data export in machine readable format. Common schema across sectors. Database of innovation with public data. User friendly search engine. Social Media share.
questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly listed as one of NDAP's planned Features in the Vision Document?
options: Automatic translation of all datasets into every scheduled Indian language
Facilitating analysis directly in tools such as R, Tableau and SAS, alongside machine-readable data export
A built-in blockchain ledger for verifying data provenance
A mobile-only app with no web interface
questions.explanation: The Vision Document's Features list includes facilitating analysis in R, Tableau and SAS and providing data export in machine-readable format, among others such as a common schema, a database of innovation, a search engine, and social media sharing. None of the other options -- automatic translation, blockchain, or mobile-only design -- appear in the document.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Features'/'Benefits' -- database of innovation
questions.source_excerpt: Showcase innovative uses and top research articles for every search result... Database of innovation with public data.
questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'database of innovation' feature described in the Vision Document?
options: To store backup copies of raw datasets in case of server failure
To showcase innovative uses of the data and top research articles alongside each search result, encouraging further research and innovation
To rank Ministries by how quickly they respond to RTI requests
To restrict access to datasets until a peer-reviewed paper cites them
questions.explanation: The 'database of innovation' feature is meant to surface innovative uses and top research articles associated with a search result, so users can see how data has already been used and be inspired to build on it -- not to serve as a backup system, an RTI ranking tool, or an access gate.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Users' panel
questions.source_excerpt: Users: Policy Makers, Journalists, Citizens, General Public, Researchers, Academics, Data Scientists, Innovators.
questions.question: The Vision Document lists NDAP's intended user groups. Which of the following is explicitly included in that list?
options: Foreign governments only
Journalists and data scientists, alongside policymakers, researchers, academics, innovators, and the general public
Only employees of NITI Aayog
Only registered software developers with an API key
questions.explanation: The document's Users panel names policymakers, journalists, citizens, the general public, researchers, academics, data scientists and innovators as NDAP's intended audience -- a deliberately broad, non-exclusive list, unlike the narrow groups described in the other options.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Governance Structure' -- High Powered Steering Committee
questions.source_excerpt: High Powered Steering Committee: A high powered inter-ministerial steering committee under the chairmanship of Vice Chairman, NITI Aayog will be set up to provide direction, oversee progress, guide on data sources, and address various inter-ministerial issues on collating data.
questions.question: Who is designated to chair the High Powered Steering Committee that oversees NDAP, according to the Vision Document's governance structure?
options: The Cabinet Secretary
The Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog
The Union Minister of Electronics and Information Technology
The Comptroller and Auditor General
questions.explanation: The Vision Document specifies that the inter-ministerial High Powered Steering Committee is chaired by the Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog, who provides direction and resolves inter-ministerial data-collation issues. The other office-holders are not named in this governance structure.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Governance Structure' -- Technical Advisory Group
questions.source_excerpt: Technical Advisory Group: A Technical Advisory Group consisting of sector and technology experts will be established to provide expert consultation. TAG will provide guidance on the development of the platform, management of data, and aligning the platform for user-needs.
questions.question: What role does the Technical Advisory Group (TAG) play within NDAP's governance structure, per the Vision Document?
options: It approves the annual Union Budget allocation for NITI Aayog
It provides expert consultation from sector and technology experts on platform development, data management, and aligning the platform to user needs
It has sole legal authority to shut down the platform if a data breach occurs
It replaces the Technology Vendor as the entity that builds and operates the platform
questions.explanation: TAG is an advisory body of sector and technology experts guiding platform development, data management, and user-need alignment -- an advisory, not an operational or budget-approval, role, and distinct from the Technology Vendor that actually builds and runs the platform.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Governance Structure' -- Project Management Unit
questions.source_excerpt: Project Management Unit: Established at NITI Aayog to coordinate with different stakeholders and manage various facets of NDAP.
questions.question: Where is NDAP's Project Management Unit (PMU) located, and what is its role, according to the Vision Document?
options: At the Ministry of Finance, to control the platform's budget only
At NITI Aayog, to coordinate with stakeholders and manage various facets of NDAP
At each State Government's IT department, run independently in every state
Outside Government, at the technology vendor's own head office
questions.explanation: The Vision Document places the PMU at NITI Aayog, tasked with coordinating stakeholders and managing NDAP's various facets -- not at the Finance Ministry, decentralised to states, or outsourced entirely to the vendor.

questions.locator: Vision Document, description of the 'Up-to-date' objective
questions.source_excerpt: NDAP will be a reliable platform for up-to-date data. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) will be developed to keep data updated. There will be regular tracking of compliance to these SOPs. Further, APIs, web-crawling and other methods will be used to keep the data fully up-to-date.
questions.question: A Ministry's dataset on NDAP has not been refreshed in over a year. Based on the Vision Document's stated approach to keeping data current, what mechanism is meant to catch and correct this?
options: Citizens must individually email the Ministry to request an update
SOPs for regular updates, with tracking of SOP compliance, backed by APIs and web-crawling to keep data current
The dataset is simply deleted from the platform after six months
NDAP has no mechanism for this; refreshing data is left entirely to each Ministry's discretion
questions.explanation: The Vision Document describes a structured 'up-to-date' mechanism: SOPs for updating data, active tracking of compliance with those SOPs, and technical means such as APIs and web-crawling to keep data current -- not an ad hoc citizen-complaint process, automatic deletion, or complete Ministry discretion.

questions.locator: Vision Document, 'Way Forward'
questions.source_excerpt: The first version of National Data and Analytics Platform is proposed to be released in 2021. NDAP is a pan-India initiative by NITI Aayog. Its success requires extensive support and cooperation of various stakeholders such as Central Ministries, State Governments and guidance from experts.
questions.question: According to the 'Way Forward' section of the Vision Document, in which year was the first version of NDAP proposed to be released?
questions.explanation: The Vision Document states that the first version of NDAP was proposed to be released in 2021, describing NDAP as a pan-India initiative requiring cooperation from Central Ministries, State Governments, and experts -- the other years are not mentioned.

questions.locator: Vision Document, synthesis of 'Challenges' and 'Approach' sections
questions.source_excerpt: Data ecosystem is incoherent due to different standards... If we can solve this, many use-cases can emerge. For example, a District Magistrate can access data across all departments for their district, easily, in one platform.
questions.question: A state government wants to replicate NDAP's District Magistrate use-case at the district level, pulling health, education, and agriculture data into one dashboard. Based on the Vision Document, which two NDAP design elements would matter most for this to work well?
options: A social media share button and a mobile app icon
A common schema with consistent geographical/temporal identifiers, and a user-friendly search engine tailored to non-technical officials
A requirement that all three departments merge into a single administrative unit
A ban on any data more than one year old
questions.explanation: Combining data from multiple departments into one usable dashboard depends on the coherence objective (a common schema and shared geographic/temporal identifiers so datasets 'speak to each other') and the user-centric objective (an accessible, user-friendly interface for officials who are not data specialists) -- not on administrative mergers, data-age bans, or social/sharing features.

questions.locator: Vision Document, overall design philosophy across 'Overview', 'Challenges' and 'Objectives'
questions.source_excerpt: All public government data should be easily accessible to all stakeholders in a user-friendly manner. Further, data across sectors should be coherent to support analysis and dissemination... Coherent: Multiple data sets are presented using a standardized schema.
questions.question: Why does the Vision Document treat 'Coherent' as a necessary objective distinct from simply publishing more data online?
options: Because coherence is a legal requirement under the Right to Information Act

Because more raw data alone does not help users if datasets use inconsistent definitions and standards, making cross-department or cross-sector analysis impossible even when the data is technically 'available'
Because coherent data takes up less server storage than incoherent data
Because the document considers data volume less important than data secrecy
questions.explanation: The document's own 'Challenges' section shows that simply having more data published does not solve the underlying problem: without shared standards for indicators, regions and time periods, datasets cannot be meaningfully combined or compared, which is exactly why 'Coherent' is called out as its own objective rather than folded into general availability. It is not framed as an RTI compliance matter, a storage-efficiency concern, or about secrecy.

questions.locator: KQF, Part II -- The Karmayogi Competency Model's three domains
questions.source_excerpt: The KCM identifies three interconnected domains of competency. Behavioural competencies, which includes dispositions, values, and interpersonal capacities... grow in importance with seniority and determine whether technical capability translates into effective public service.
questions.question: According to the Karmayogi Quality Framework, why do behavioural competencies matter increasingly at senior levels of the civil service?
options: Because senior officers no longer need functional or domain competencies at all

Because behavioural competencies -- dispositions, values, and interpersonal capacities -- determine whether an officer's technical capability actually translates into effective public service as their leadership responsibility grows
Because behavioural competencies are only assessed during recruitment, never afterward
Because senior officers are exempt from the Karmayogi Competency Model
questions.explanation: The KQF states that behavioural competencies grow in importance with seniority precisely because they determine whether technical skill converts into real leadership effectiveness -- functional and domain competencies remain necessary, they are simply not sufficient on their own at senior, higher-influence roles.

questions.locator: KQF, Part II -- Administrative Role Family dimension
questions.source_excerpt: Administrative Role Family... Initiator: originates files and actions. Reviewer: examines and recommends. Decision Maker: approves, commits resources. Strategic Leader: sets direction, manages performance. Policy Maker: formulates and advises on legislation.
questions.question: The Karmayogi Quality Framework calibrates course design partly by 'Administrative Role Family.' Which role in that dimension is described as setting direction and managing performance?
options: Initiator
Reviewer
Strategic Leader
Policy Maker
questions.explanation: Within the Administrative Role Family dimension, the 'Strategic Leader' role is the one defined as setting direction and managing performance, distinct from an Initiator (originates files), a Reviewer (examines and recommends), and a Policy Maker (formulates and advises on legislation).

questions.locator: KQF, Part II -- Decision Complexity (S-T-O) lens
questions.source_excerpt: Strategic: policy design, systems thinking, cross-sectoral influence, and leadership in complexity.
questions.question: In the Karmayogi Quality Framework's S-T-O (Strategic-Tactical-Operational) lens on decision complexity, what specifically characterizes the 'Strategic' level?
options: Procedural accuracy and rule application in citizen-facing execution
Cross-programme problem-solving and delivery ownership within a single team
Policy design, systems thinking, cross-sectoral influence, and leadership in complexity
Filling in standard forms with no room for judgement
questions.explanation: The Strategic level of the S-T-O lens is defined by policy design, systems thinking, cross-sectoral influence, and leadership in complexity -- procedural accuracy belongs to the Operational level and cross-programme delivery ownership to the Tactical level.

questions.locator: KQF, Foreword
questions.source_excerpt: This is what Mission Karmayogi calls, the shift from a rule orientation to a role orientation. Rules are necessary but never sufficient... It is in that space [between rule and situation] that character and competence determine whether a citizen is served with dignity or denied with indifference.
questions.question: The KQF Foreword argues that 'the real work of governance happens in the space between what the rule says and what the situation demands.' What leadership implication does it draw from this?
options: That rules should be abolished entirely in favour of officer discretion
That character and competence in that discretionary space determine whether citizens are served with dignity, so leadership development cannot rely on rule-compliance alone
That only the most junior officials ever face this discretionary space
That this space is irrelevant to how learning on iGOT should be designed
questions.explanation: The Foreword's point is not to abolish rules but to argue that rules alone are insufficient: exercising sound judgement in the gap between rule and situation requires character and competence, which is exactly why leadership-relevant learning must go beyond rule-compliance training -- a theme carried through the rest of the framework, not confined to junior officials.

questions.locator: KQF, Part V -- Governance Architecture, Cadre Controlling Authorities
questions.source_excerpt: Cadre Controlling Authorities (CCAs): Career integrators -- set competency benchmarks, align learning with career progression, embed learning in appraisals, and use data for evidence-based decisions.
questions.question: Within the KQF's governance architecture, what distinct leadership-development function do Cadre Controlling Authorities (CCAs) perform that Karmayogi Bharat (the platform operator) does not?
options: They build and host the iGOT technology platform
They act as 'career integrators', setting competency benchmarks and embedding learning outcomes into career progression and appraisals
They author individual course content for every Ministry
They audit the financial accounts of the Capacity Building Commission
questions.explanation: CCAs are explicitly framed as career integrators: they connect learning to career progression by setting competency benchmarks and embedding evidence of learning into appraisals -- a people-development and career-leadership function distinct from Karmayogi Bharat's platform-operations role or CBC's standard-setting role.

questions.locator: KQF, Part II -- Foundation of the Karmayogi Competency Model
questions.source_excerpt: This calibration is anchored in competencies; behavioural and functional as specified in the Karmayogi Competency Model (KCM), and domain competencies as defined by each MDO in reference to the KCM.
questions.question: Under the Karmayogi Competency Model (KCM), who is responsible for defining domain competencies (as opposed to behavioural and functional competencies)?
options: Each Ministry/Department/Organisation (MDO), in reference to the KCM
The learner themselves, through self-assessment
The Capacity Building Commission alone, with no MDO involvement
The Union Public Service Commission during recruitment
questions.explanation: The KQF states that while behavioural and functional competencies are specified centrally in the KCM, domain competencies -- the technical knowledge specific to a sector -- are defined by each MDO in reference to the KCM, not by the learner, the CBC alone, or the UPSC.

questions.locator: KQF, Part V -- Accountability table
questions.source_excerpt: Content Providers: Execution engine. Build courses to the approved Design-from-Work Declaration. Accountable for the quality signal their courses generate over their full operational life.
questions.question: A leadership-development course consistently receives an Amber rating on its Course Performance Index over several months. Based on the KQF's accountability model, who bears primary responsibility for remediating the course?
options: The individual learners who enrolled in it
The Content Provider that built and remains accountable for the course's quality signal over its full operational life
The Quality Advisory Council, since it is a regulatory body
The Cadre Controlling Authority of an unrelated cadre
questions.explanation: Content Providers are described as the 'execution engine' accountable for their course's quality signal across its entire operational life, including responding to persistent Amber/Red ratings -- the Quality Advisory Council is explicitly an advisory, not regulatory, forum, and neither learners nor an unrelated CCA hold this responsibility.

questions.locator: KQF, Part III Overview -- the Six Stages table
questions.source_excerpt: 01 Discover -- Who is this learner? ... 02 Design -- Is it built from real work? ... Gate: Capability Blueprint reviewed before development begins.
questions.question: A senior officer designing a leadership course skips the Discover and Design gates, going straight to content production because 'leadership is leadership everywhere.' Which KQF principle does this violate?
options: Nothing -- the KQF only applies gates to technical, not leadership, courses
The requirement that every course be anchored in a specific work context and calibrated to decision complexity, decision archetype, and administrative role family before development begins
The rule that leadership courses must be at least 60 minutes long
The rule that only the Capacity Building Commission may design leadership courses
questions.explanation: The KQF's Discover and Design gates exist precisely because quality course design 'requires that every course be precisely calibrated to the specific context of its intended learner' -- decision complexity, archetype and role family all differ even within 'leadership' -- so skipping these gates undermines a core, non-negotiable principle of the framework, which applies to every competency domain, not just technical ones.

questions.locator: PIB press release, institutional framework
questions.source_excerpt: The Union Cabinet... has approved launching of a National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (NPCSCB) with the following institutional framework:- (i) Prime Minister's Public Human Resources (HR) Council, (ii) Capacity Building Commission...
questions.question: Which body sits at the apex of the NPCSCB institutional framework announced by the Cabinet, chaired by the Prime Minister?
options: The Capacity Building Commission
The Prime Minister's Public Human Resources (HR) Council
The Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)
The Coordination Unit headed by the Cabinet Secretary
questions.explanation: The press release lists the Prime Minister's Public HR Council first among the four institutional bodies, and later describes it as the apex body under the Prime Minister's chairmanship providing strategic direction -- the Capacity Building Commission, the SPV, and the Coordination Unit are distinct, subordinate bodies with narrower mandates.

questions.locator: PIB press release, 'Background'
questions.source_excerpt: A Public Human Resources Council comprising of select Union Ministers, Chief Ministers, eminent public HR practitioners, thinkers, global thought leaders and Public Service functionaries under the Chairmanship of Hon'ble Prime Minister will serve as the apex body for providing strategic direction to the task of Civil Services Reform and capacity building.
questions.question: What is distinctive about the composition of the PM's Public HR Council, as announced in the Cabinet press release?
options: It is composed entirely of serving IAS officers

It draws together Union Ministers, Chief Ministers, HR practitioners, thinkers, global thought leaders, and public service functionaries under the PM's chairmanship -- a deliberately cross-sector strategic leadership body
It is a purely technical body of software engineers who maintain the iGOT platform
It consists only of retired civil servants
questions.explanation: The Council's composition is explicitly cross-sector and cross-level -- Ministers, Chief Ministers, HR practitioners, thought leaders and functionaries -- reflecting its role as an apex strategic-direction body for civil service reform, not a narrow technical, retired-officer, or single-service body.

questions.locator: PIB press release, 'Objectives' -- role of the Capacity Building Commission
questions.source_excerpt: The role of Commission will be as under- To assist the PM Public Human Resources Council in approving the Annual Capacity Building Plans... To exercise functional supervision over all Central Training Institutions... To suggest policy interventions required in the areas of HR Management and Capacity Building to the Government.
questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a role of the Capacity Building Commission in the Cabinet's announcement?
options: Directly hiring and firing civil servants
Assisting the PM's Public HR Council in approving Annual Capacity Building Plans and exercising functional supervision over Central Training Institutions
Setting the annual Union Budget
Conducting the Civil Services Examination in place of the UPSC
questions.explanation: The press release assigns the Commission roles such as assisting the PM Council on Capacity Building Plans, functional supervision of Central Training Institutions, standardisation recommendations, and policy suggestions on HR management -- not hiring/firing authority, budget-setting, or examination duties, which remain with other bodies.

questions.locator: PIB press release, 'Salient Features' -- rules-based to roles-based HR
questions.source_excerpt: Supporting Transition from 'Rules based' to 'Roles based' HR Management. Aligning work allocation of civil servants by matching their competencies to the requirements of the post.
questions.question: A department currently assigns civil servants to posts purely by seniority and rotation schedule, without reference to their demonstrated competencies. Which core guiding principle of Mission Karmayogi does this practice run counter to?
options: The transition from 'rules based' to 'roles based' HR management, which calls for aligning work allocation to an officer's competencies against the requirements of the post
The requirement that iGOT courses be under 20 minutes long
The financial cap of Rs 510.86 crore on the programme
The rule restricting the SPV to a not-for-profit structure
questions.explanation: Mission Karmayogi's guiding principle of shifting from rules-based to roles-based HR management is specifically about matching work allocation to competencies rather than seniority or rotation alone -- the other options describe unrelated operational or financial details of the programme, not this HR-management principle.

questions.locator: PIB press release, 'Objectives'
questions.source_excerpt: Mission Karmayogi aims to prepare the Indian Civil Servant for the future by making him more creative, constructive, imaginative, innovative, proactive, professional, progressive, energetic, enabling, transparent and technology-enabled.
questions.question: According to the press release, Mission Karmayogi aims to prepare the civil servant for the future by cultivating which kind of qualities?
options: Strict seniority-based conformity and risk-aversion
A cluster of qualities including creative, proactive, professional, enabling, transparent and technology-enabled
Exclusively technical, IT-specific skills with no behavioural component
Qualities relevant only to officers posted abroad
questions.explanation: The press release lists a broad cluster of qualities -- creative, constructive, imaginative, innovative, proactive, professional, progressive, energetic, enabling, transparent, and technology-enabled -- explicitly aimed at future-readiness, not seniority-based conformity, a narrow technical focus, or a foreign-posting-specific remit.

questions.locator: PIB press release, institutional framework and Coordination Unit
questions.source_excerpt: (iv) Coordination Unit headed by the Cabinet Secretary.
questions.question: Why does the NPCSCB institutional framework place a Coordination Unit headed by the Cabinet Secretary alongside the PM's HR Council, the Capacity Building Commission, and the SPV?
options: Because the Cabinet Secretary alone approves individual officers' course grades

Because a programme spanning strategic direction (PM Council), standard-setting (Commission), and platform operations (SPV) needs a senior cross-government coordination point to keep these separate institutional roles aligned
Because the SPV is legally required to report only to the Cabinet Secretary and no one else
Because the Capacity Building Commission cannot function without the Cabinet Secretary's daily sign-off
questions.explanation: With strategic direction, standard-setting, and platform operations distributed across three different bodies, a Coordination Unit under the Cabinet Secretary -- the seniormost civil servant with cross-ministry reach -- provides the connective coordination the multi-body structure needs; the other options invent authority relationships the press release does not state.

questions.locator: PIB press release, 'Salient Features' -- FRAC approach
questions.source_excerpt: To calibrate all Civil Service positions to a Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies (FRACs) approach and to create and deliver learning content relevant to the identified FRACs in every Government entity.
questions.question: What is the purpose of calibrating every Civil Service position to a 'Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies' (FRACs), as described in the Cabinet announcement?
options: To determine each officer's retirement age
To make explicit what a given post actually requires, so that relevant learning content can be created and delivered against those identified needs
To rank Ministries by budget size
To eliminate the need for any performance appraisal
questions.explanation: FRACs exist to define each position's roles, activities and required competencies explicitly, which then lets the system create and deliver learning content targeted at those specific needs -- not to set retirement ages, rank budgets, or replace appraisals.

questions.locator: PIB press release, 'Background' and 'Salient Features' read together
questions.source_excerpt: A transformational change in Civil Service Capacity is proposed to be affected by organically linking the transformation of work culture, strengthening public institutions and adopting modern technology... Supporting Transition from 'Rules based' to 'Roles based' HR Management.
questions.question: A Ministry wants to adopt only the iGOT technology platform from Mission Karmayogi, without changing how it allocates work or evaluates competencies. Based on the programme's own stated design, why would this partial adoption likely fall short of its intended leadership and HR transformation?
options: Because iGOT only works if a Ministry also purchases separate hardware from the SPV

Because the Background explicitly frames the reform as organically linking work-culture transformation, institution-strengthening, and technology together, so technology alone without the rules-to-roles HR shift leaves the core competency-based work-allocation change unaddressed
Because the press release states iGOT cannot legally be used without Cabinet approval each time
Because Mission Karmayogi applies only to State Governments, not the technology layer of Central Ministries
questions.explanation: The programme is explicitly designed as an organic link between work-culture change, institutional strengthening and technology adoption -- adopting only the technology (iGOT) while leaving work allocation and appraisal practices untouched would miss the rules-to-roles HR shift that is the programme's central leadership and HR-management objective, not a hardware, approval, or Central/State jurisdiction issue.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 2 -- Format of Citizen's/Client's Charter, the nine sections
questions.source_excerpt: The Citizen's Charter for a Ministry/Department should contain the following nine sections: Cover Page, Vision, Mission, Service Standards, Grievance Redress Mechanism, Stakeholders/Clients, Responsibility Centers, Indicative expectations from service recipients, Month and Year for next review of the charter.
questions.question: How many mandatory sections does the DARPG guideline prescribe for a Citizen's/Client's Charter, and which of the following is one of them?
options: Five sections, including a 'Budget Summary'
Nine sections, including 'Indicative expectations from service recipients'
Three sections, limited to Vision, Mission, and Contact Details
Twelve sections, including 'Employee Grievance Redressal for HR Matters'
questions.explanation: The guideline specifies exactly nine sections -- Cover Page, Vision, Mission, Service Standards, Grievance Redress Mechanism, Stakeholders/Clients, Responsibility Centers, Indicative expectations from service recipients, and the next review date -- not five, three, or twelve, and there is no separate 'Budget Summary' section.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 1 -- Concept of Citizen's/Client's Charter
questions.source_excerpt: The Citizen's/Client's Charter is a written declaration by a Government department that highlights the standards of service delivery that it subscribes to... The basic thrust... is to render public services citizen centric by making them demand driven rather than supply driven.
questions.question: What is the 'basic thrust' of a Citizen's/Client's Charter, according to the DARPG guideline?
options: To make public services demand driven rather than supply driven, by publicly committing to service standards
To create a legally enforceable contract citizens can sue on in a civil court
To reduce the total number of services a department is required to offer
To replace the need for a Public Grievance Redress Mechanism entirely
questions.explanation: The guideline states the Charter's basic thrust is making services citizen-centric and demand driven rather than supply driven, through public commitments to service standards -- it explicitly notes the Charter is not enforceable in a court of law, does not aim to shrink service scope, and works alongside, not instead of, the grievance mechanism.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 1 -- Citizens versus Clients
questions.source_excerpt: Citizens are... generally referred to as external clients... It cannot be presumed that all citizens are literate or understand the official language, and it may be necessary to communicate with them in the local language also. Clients... are generally referred to as internal clients... it is presumed that all clients are literate and communicating with them in the official language of the service provider agency is sufficient.
questions.question: Why does the guideline draw a communication-relevant distinction between 'Citizens' and 'Clients' when a department designs its Charter?
options: Because citizens are assumed to possibly be non-literate or unfamiliar with the official language, requiring local-language communication, while clients (other government agencies/employees) are presumed literate in the official language
Because the term 'Client' refers only to paying customers of a government-run business
Because citizens are legally barred from filing grievances, unlike clients
Because the distinction determines which department gets a bigger printing budget for its Charter
questions.explanation: The guideline draws this distinction specifically for communication design: citizens, as external members of the public, cannot be assumed literate or fluent in the official language, so local-language communication may be necessary, whereas clients, being part of government, are presumed literate in the official language -- the other options misstate or invent unrelated rationales.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 2 -- mandatory requirements, bilingual publication
questions.source_excerpt: The Charter is to be made in bilingual version as per requirements of the Official Languages Act and approved by Minister-in-charge before publication... In offices located in Region 'C' it should also be published in the local language in addition to English and Hindi.
questions.question: What language requirements does the DARPG guideline impose on a published Citizen's Charter?
options: It may be published in any single language the department prefers
It must be bilingual (English and Hindi) per the Official Languages Act, and offices in Region 'C' must additionally publish it in the local language
It must be published only in English, to maintain a uniform national standard
It must be translated into all 22 scheduled languages regardless of where the office is located
questions.explanation: The guideline mandates a bilingual Charter under the Official Languages Act, with an additional local-language version required for offices in Region 'C' -- not a single-language, English-only, or all-22-languages requirement.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 2 -- mandatory requirements, dissemination
questions.source_excerpt: After publication twenty copies are required to be sent to the Librarian, Parliament Library... The Charter needs to be placed on the Ministry/Department's website... A single page containing extracts of main services and standards from the charter can be displayed at the Reception and other prominent places.
questions.question: Besides placing the Charter on the department's website, what other dissemination steps does the guideline require or recommend?
options: Sending 20 copies to the Parliament Library and displaying a single-page extract of main services and standards at the Reception and other prominent places
Emailing the Charter individually to every registered taxpayer
Publishing the Charter exclusively as a mobile app, with no printed or web version
Filing the Charter with the Election Commission before every general election
questions.explanation: The guideline requires sending 20 copies to the Parliament Library and recommends a single-page reception-area display of main services and standards, alongside media publicity where warranted -- it does not require individual taxpayer emails, an app-only format, or Election Commission filing.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 2 -- 'Concluding Remarks'
questions.source_excerpt: It is imperative that the Citizen's Charter be kept user friendly as well as concise by including all the necessary information, but without clutter, rhetoric, and very lengthy information which may be daunting for the average service recipient. ... it can be provided separately on the website in another document.
questions.question: A department drafts a 40-page Citizen's Charter full of departmental jargon and legal cross-references, aiming to be exhaustive. How does this align with the guideline's communication principles?
options: It aligns perfectly, since exhaustiveness is the guideline's top priority

It conflicts with the guideline, which calls for a concise, user-friendly Charter without clutter or lengthy rhetoric, recommending that very detailed information instead be hosted separately on the website with a reference in the Charter
It conflicts with the guideline only because 40 pages exceeds a hard legal page limit
It aligns with the guideline as long as the Charter is printed in colour
questions.explanation: The guideline explicitly warns against clutter, rhetoric, and lengthy content that could overwhelm the average service recipient, recommending that very detailed material be hosted separately online with a simple reference in the Charter -- there is no stated hard page-limit rule, and print colour is irrelevant to the underlying communication principle.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 1 -- definition of grievances
questions.source_excerpt: Grievances are expressions of resentment against specific acts of omission or commission that are wrong or perceived as wrong, and requiring corrective action to be taken... grievances include complaints by service recipients against non-delivery of services as expected... but do not include requests for service delivery in the normal course.
questions.question: Under the DARPG guideline, which of the following would NOT count as a 'grievance' for Sevottam compliance purposes?
options: A complaint that a promised service was not delivered as expected
A routine, normal-course request for a service the citizen has not yet received (with no complaint of wrongdoing)
A complaint against a specific act of omission perceived as wrong
A complaint requiring corrective action by the department
questions.explanation: The guideline explicitly excludes ordinary requests for service delivery in the normal course from the definition of a grievance -- a grievance requires an expression of resentment against a specific act of omission or commission perceived as wrong, which the other three options describe.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 1 -- CPGRAMS
questions.source_excerpt: One such system extensively being used in the Central Government Ministries/Departments is the Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS)... The citizens can lodge their grievances from any internet facility on www.pgportal.nic.in.
questions.question: What is CPGRAMS, as described in the DARPG guideline?
options: A citizen feedback survey conducted only once every five years
An internet-based system (accessible via pgportal.nic.in) for lodging, forwarding, and monitoring public grievances across Central Government Ministries and Departments
A court established specifically to hear service-delivery disputes
A private company hired to handle all government grievance redress
questions.explanation: CPGRAMS is described as an internet-based tool, accessible at pgportal.nic.in, for lodging, forwarding, and monitoring grievances across Ministries and Departments -- not a periodic survey, a court, or a private contractor.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 4 -- classification criteria for grievances
questions.source_excerpt: The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances has provided five broad suggestive criteria under which the Ministry/Department can categorize their grievances: Charter related, Policy related, Personnel related, Pensioners' related, Vigilance related.
questions.question: Which set of categories does DARPG's guideline suggest for classifying grievances so that departments can route them appropriately?
options: Urgent, Routine, Low-priority
Charter related, Policy related, Personnel related, Pensioners' related, Vigilance related
Digital, Physical, Telephonic
Central, State, Local
questions.explanation: The guideline's five suggested classification criteria are Charter related, Policy related, Personnel related, Pensioners' related, and Vigilance related -- the other option sets describe plausible-sounding categorisation schemes that the guideline does not actually use.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 4 -- 'Communication to complainant'
questions.source_excerpt: At the time of acknowledgement, the complainant should be provided with: a. Grievance number... b. Expected time of redress (Prescribed maximum time limit for completion of redress is three months) c. If not addressed within expected time, action to be taken by complainant.
questions.question: A citizen's grievance has just been formally received and acknowledged by a department. According to the guideline, what specific information must the department communicate to the complainant at this point?
options: Only a verbal apology, with no written record
A grievance number, the expected time of redress (up to a maximum of three months), and what action the complainant can take if that time is exceeded
The complainant's own Aadhaar number, for department records
Nothing, since acknowledgement itself is optional under the guideline
questions.explanation: At acknowledgement, the guideline requires providing a grievance number, the expected redress time (capped at a maximum of three months), and next steps if that time is exceeded -- not a verbal-only response, a request for the complainant's Aadhaar number, or an optional/no-communication approach.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 4 -- communication when redress is delayed
questions.source_excerpt: If the grievance is not redressed within the expected time, the complainant should be provided with the following information... a. Information on reasons for delay b. Updated expected time of redress c. If not addressed within expected time, action to be taken by complainant.
questions.question: A grievance has now exceeded its originally communicated redress timeline. What does the guideline say the department must proactively communicate to the complainant?
options: Nothing further, since the original acknowledgement already covers this
The reasons for the delay, an updated expected redress time, and what further action the complainant can take if the new deadline is also missed
A formal legal notice threatening penalties against the complainant
A request that the complainant resubmit the grievance from scratch
questions.explanation: The guideline requires proactive follow-up communication when a redress deadline is missed: reasons for delay, an updated timeline, and further escalation options -- not silence, a penalty notice against the complainant, or forcing resubmission.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 4 -- final redress communication
questions.source_excerpt: At the time of final redress, the complainant should be provided with the following information by the office responsible for redress of the grievances: d. Action taken for redress e. If not satisfied with the redress action, avenues for pursuing the matter further.
questions.question: When a grievance is finally resolved, what must the closing communication to the complainant include, per the guideline?
options: Only a case-closed stamp with no further detail
The action taken for redress, and the avenues available to the complainant if they remain unsatisfied with that action
A survey asking the complainant to rate the officer's promotion prospects
A demand that the complainant pay a processing fee before the case can close
questions.explanation: Final redress communication must state the action taken and the avenues for further escalation if the complainant is unsatisfied -- not a bare closure stamp, an unrelated promotion survey, or a fee demand.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 4 -- Level of Responsibility for Redress
questions.source_excerpt: In order to ensure that grievances are addressed within the prescribed time norms, the GRM should define the levels of responsibility for redress... In case the grievance is not redressed at a particular defined level then an avenue should be available to the complainant to approach the next higher authority. The responsible officials at each level should alert their next superior official well in time.
questions.question: Why does the guideline require both a defined escalation ladder for complainants AND an internal 'alert the next superior official' step for staff?
options: Because escalation ladders are a legal formality with no real communication purpose

Because effective grievance communication needs two channels working together: an external escalation path so the complainant is never stuck without recourse, and an internal early-warning path so supervisors intervene before deadlines are actually missed
Because only one of the two is ever actually used in practice
Because the internal alert replaces the need to ever tell the complainant anything
questions.explanation: The guideline pairs an external escalation avenue for the complainant with an internal early-warning obligation on staff so that supervisors can intervene proactively, not just after a citizen complains again -- the two channels serve complementary communication purposes, not a redundant or complainant-excluding one.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 3 -- Step 3, stakeholder consultation planning
questions.source_excerpt: Prepare a detailed survey plan including information on whether it will be a survey on mail, or data will be collected through open house discussions, or through open advertisement, the timelines for the survey, number of beneficiaries to be surveyed, location... This will help in scheduling stakeholder consultation meets or receiving stakeholder inputs.
questions.question: Which methods does the guideline mention for gathering citizen input on service standards before finalising a Citizen's Charter?
options: Only anonymous online polls, since in-person methods are prohibited
Mail surveys, open house discussions, and open advertisements, among other consultation tools
A single national referendum held once per Charter cycle
Consultation is not permitted; Charters are drafted solely by department officials
questions.explanation: The guideline lists mail surveys, open house discussions and open advertisements (among other tools) as ways to gather stakeholder input on service standards -- it does not restrict consultation to online-only polls, mandate a referendum, or forbid stakeholder input altogether.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 3 -- Step 8, internal staff communication
questions.source_excerpt: Task 1: Send communication to all staff. Send a communication to all staff members enclosing the Charter and advising them on how they will be delivering services in accordance with standards laid down in the Charter. Task 2: Conduct training/orientation sessions for staff on Citizen's Charter.
questions.question: After a Charter is finalized and published externally, what internal communication step does the guideline require before staff can be expected to deliver against it?
options: None -- staff are expected to infer the Charter's contents from the published website
Sending the Charter to all staff with guidance on how they must deliver services against it, followed by training/orientation sessions
A one-time announcement in a staff newsletter, with no training required
Making the Charter available only to the Head of Department, who need not share it further
questions.explanation: The guideline requires an explicit internal step: distributing the Charter to all staff with delivery guidance, followed by training and orientation sessions -- not silence, a passive newsletter mention, or restricting the Charter to the Head of Department alone.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 3 -- Step 6, Charter approval process
questions.source_excerpt: Task 4: Make Hindi version of final charter. A public document is required to be published in bilingual version... Task 5: Get the Charter approved by Minister-in-charge. Approval of the Charter in bilingual version by the Minister-in-charge is mandatory.
questions.question: A department finalizes its Citizen's Charter in English, gets it approved by the Secretary, and publishes it immediately to meet a deadline. What communication-process requirement of the guideline has it skipped?
options: Nothing was skipped; Secretary-level approval of an English-only Charter fully satisfies the guideline
Preparing the mandatory bilingual (Hindi) version and obtaining approval specifically from the Minister-in-charge before publication
The requirement to translate the Charter into all state languages before any publication
The requirement to publish the Charter only after the next Union Budget is passed
questions.explanation: The guideline makes both the bilingual (Hindi) version and sign-off specifically by the Minister-in-charge mandatory before publication -- Secretary-level approval of an English-only Charter satisfies neither requirement, and there is no all-state-languages or Budget-timing rule.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 1 -- background of Sevottam-compliance mandatory indicators
questions.source_excerpt: The High Power Committee (HPC) on Government Performance chaired by the Cabinet Secretary decided that all RFDs for 2010-2011 will include the following mandatory success indicators: Create a Sevottam compliant system to implement, monitor and review Citizen's Charter... Create a Sevottam Compliant system to redress and monitor public Grievances.
questions.question: Why were Citizen's Charter and Grievance Redress Mechanism indicators added as mandatory items to departmental Results-Framework Documents (RFDs), per the guideline's background?
options: Because the High Power Committee on Government Performance, chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, decided all RFDs for 2010-11 would include Sevottam-compliance as a mandatory success indicator
Because the Supreme Court ordered it in a landmark judgment
Because state governments unilaterally added it without central direction
Because it was a requirement imposed by an international lending agency
questions.explanation: The guideline's background section attributes this mandatory inclusion to a decision of the High Power Committee on Government Performance, chaired by the Cabinet Secretary -- not a court order, a state-level initiative, or an international agency requirement.

questions.locator: Guidelines, Chapter 2 -- Service Standards section design
questions.source_excerpt: Service Standards... Main Services include services that are being provided on a regular basis... Departmental Services rendered occasionally under exceptional or extraordinary circumstances should not be a part of Main Services. These should also be aligned with the GRM processes.
questions.question: Why does the guideline deliberately exclude occasional, exceptional-circumstance services from the Charter's 'Main Services' table, rather than listing every service a department ever performs?
options: Because exceptional services are legally confidential and cannot be disclosed to citizens

Because the Charter is meant to communicate clear, dependable standards for the services most citizens routinely rely on, and cluttering it with rarely-invoked exceptional services would undermine that clarity and make the document harder to use
Because exceptional services never have measurable standards of any kind
Because only Main Services are eligible for RTI requests
questions.explanation: This design choice follows the guideline's broader communication principle of keeping the Charter clear and usable: focusing on routinely-availed 'Main Services' keeps the document meaningful for the average citizen, while occasional exceptional services would add clutter without matching that goal -- confidentiality, measurability, and RTI eligibility are not the stated reasons.

questions.locator: KQF, Part I -- Seven Commitments table, seventh commitment
questions.source_excerpt: 7 Ethical & Values Alignment: Constitutional values in course design. Citizen at the last mile (antyodaya) visible in scenarios. Ethical dilemma mandatory at every level.
questions.question: What three concrete requirements does the KQF's seventh commitment, 'Ethical & Values Alignment', place on every course?
options: A 5-second load time, 720p video, and offline access
Constitutional values embedded in course design, the citizen at the last mile (antyodaya) visible in scenarios, and a mandatory ethical dilemma at every level
A minimum of 70% pass threshold and remediation pathways instead of retakes
Mandatory SME review and a 12-month content review cycle
questions.explanation: The seventh commitment specifically requires embedding constitutional values, making the citizen at the last mile (antyodaya) visible in scenarios, and building in a mandatory ethical dilemma at every level -- the other options describe requirements from different commitments (technology standards, assessment design, and content accuracy respectively).

questions.locator: KQF, Part I -- 'Why Seven?'
questions.source_excerpt: The seventh that mentions ethics and values is what makes iGOT something more than a training catalogue. It insists that learning on this platform is civic formation, not compliance training.
questions.question: According to the KQF, what distinguishes the seventh commitment (Ethics & Values Alignment) from the first six commitments?
options: It is the only commitment that applies to Group A officers
It is what makes iGOT 'something more than a training catalogue' by insisting learning is civic formation, not mere compliance training
It is the only commitment with a numeric pass threshold
It is optional, unlike the other six commitments
questions.explanation: The KQF explicitly frames the ethics commitment as the one that elevates iGOT beyond a training catalogue into civic formation -- it is not restricted to Group A officers, does not introduce a numeric threshold (that is the fourth, assessment, commitment), and is stated as an ongoing commitment like the other six, not an optional add-on.

questions.locator: KQF, Part I -- seventh commitment, antyodaya requirement
questions.source_excerpt: Citizen at the last mile (antyodaya) visible in scenarios.
questions.question: A course on subsidy disbursement uses only abstract, high-level policy language and never depicts an actual citizen receiving or being denied a benefit. Which KQF requirement does this course fail to meet?
options: The technology standard requiring 720p video
The seventh commitment's requirement that the citizen at the last mile (antyodaya) be visible in scenarios
The requirement for a Competency Coverage Matrix
The requirement for offline access
questions.explanation: The seventh commitment specifically requires that scenarios make the citizen at the last mile visible, so an abstract, citizen-absent course on subsidy disbursement fails this ethics-and-values requirement -- it is unrelated to video resolution, competency mapping, or offline access, which are separate commitments.

questions.locator: KQF, Foreword
questions.source_excerpt: That question is at the heart of the Karmayogi Quality Framework... Before any course is built, its author must answer a simple question, 'what specific work decisions will this course help a public official make better'? If that question cannot be answered clearly, the course should not be built. This is not a bureaucratic gate but an ethical one.
questions.question: Why does the KQF Foreword describe the 'work-decision' question as 'not a bureaucratic gate but an ethical one'?
options: Because failing to answer it clearly means public money is spent on learning that will not actually improve how officials serve citizens -- treated as a matter of ethical responsibility, not mere procedural compliance
Because the question is asked only by the Ethics Committee and no one else
Because answering it wrongly is a criminal offence under the CCS Conduct Rules
Because it only applies to courses about the Constitution
questions.explanation: The Foreword frames unclear work-anchoring as an ethical failure because building a course that cannot demonstrably improve real work decisions wastes public resources meant to improve citizen-facing governance -- it is not restricted to an 'Ethics Committee', is not framed as a criminal matter under the Conduct Rules, and is not limited to constitutional-topic courses.

questions.locator: KQF, Executive Summary and Part I
questions.source_excerpt: Quality is not a destination. It is a discipline. And it begins with the willingness to keep asking, 'Is the learning we are offering making our people better placed to serve the public'?
questions.question: How does the KQF frame the relationship between 'quality' and 'ethics' in civil service learning?
options: As entirely separate concerns handled by different teams with no overlap
As linked through a continuous discipline of asking whether learning genuinely helps public officials serve the public better, rather than treating quality as a one-time checklist
As a relationship that only matters for courses rated 'Red' on the Course Performance Index
As irrelevant to each other, since ethics is covered only in mandatory dilemmas
questions.explanation: The KQF frames quality as an ongoing discipline centred on whether learning actually improves public service to citizens, which is inseparable from the ethical purpose the seventh commitment articulates -- it is not siloed by team, not limited to Red-rated courses, and not confined only to the mandatory-dilemma requirement.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 3(1) -- General
questions.source_excerpt: Every Government servant shall at all times-- (i) maintain absolute integrity; (ii) maintain devotion to duty; ... (vi) maintain high ethical standards and honesty; (vii) maintain political neutrality...
questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly listed among a Government servant's general duties under Rule 3(1) of the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964?
options: Maintaining absolute integrity and political neutrality at all times
Joining the ruling political party to demonstrate loyalty
Publicly criticising any government policy the officer personally disagrees with
Prioritising personal financial gain over public interest whenever legally possible
questions.explanation: Rule 3(1) requires Government servants to maintain absolute integrity and political neutrality, among other duties -- the other options directly contradict Rule 3(1)'s requirements on political neutrality, other rules on criticism of government, and its explicit prohibition on deriving personal financial or material benefit.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 3(1)(xiii)-(xv)
questions.source_excerpt: (xiii) declare any private interests relating to his public duties and take steps to resolve any conflicts in a way that protects the public interest; ... (xv) not misuse his position as civil servant and not take decisions in order to derive financial or material benefits for himself, his family or his friends.
questions.question: What does Rule 3(1) of the CCS Conduct Rules require a Government servant to do when a private interest could conflict with their public duty?
options: Ignore the private interest as long as no one else notices
Declare the private interest and take steps to resolve any conflict in a way that protects the public interest
Transfer the decision entirely to a family member to avoid personal involvement
Resign from the post immediately, since conflicts of interest cannot be managed
questions.explanation: Rule 3(1)(xiii) requires declaration of private interests and active steps to resolve conflicts in favour of the public interest -- it does not permit silent non-disclosure, delegation to a family member (which would itself risk violating the rule against benefiting family), or an automatic resignation requirement.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 3-C -- Prohibition of sexual harassment of working women
questions.source_excerpt: (1) No Government servant shall indulge in any act of sexual harassment of any woman at any work place. (2) Every Government servant who is incharge of a work place shall take appropriate steps to prevent sexual harassment to any woman at the work place.
questions.question: Under Rule 3-C of the CCS Conduct Rules, what obligation falls specifically on a Government servant who is in charge of a workplace (e.g. a supervisor or office head)?
options: No obligation beyond their own personal conduct
To take appropriate steps to prevent sexual harassment of any woman at that workplace, in addition to not engaging in it themselves
To personally investigate and adjudicate every complaint without involving any committee
To report only complaints that come from women who are permanent Government employees
questions.explanation: Rule 3-C(2) places an affirmative, workplace-wide prevention duty on anyone in charge of a workplace, going beyond just refraining from harassment themselves -- it does not require them to personally adjudicate every case unilaterally, and Rule 3-C's definition of 'workplace' and 'woman' is not limited to permanent employees.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 4 -- Employment of near relatives in Companies or firms
questions.source_excerpt: No Class I Officer shall, except with the previous sanction of the Government, permit his son, daughter or other dependant, to accept employment in any company or firm with which he has official dealings or in any other company or firm having official dealings with the Government.
questions.question: An officer's official duties involve regular dealings with a private firm. That firm now offers the officer's daughter a job. What does Rule 4 require before she can accept it?
options: Nothing; family members' employment decisions are entirely outside the Conduct Rules
The officer must obtain the previous sanction of the Government before she accepts employment with a firm he has official dealings with (or urgently report it if sanction cannot be awaited)
The officer must resign from his post before she can accept the job
The firm must first stop all official dealings with the Government permanently
questions.explanation: Rule 4 requires a Class I officer to obtain prior Government sanction before a dependant accepts employment with a firm the officer has official dealings with, allowing provisional acceptance with prompt reporting only where sanction cannot be awaited -- it does not exempt family employment altogether, require resignation, or require the firm to sever all Government dealings.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 8 -- Connection with press or other media
questions.source_excerpt: No Government servant shall, except with the previous sanction of the Government, own wholly or in part, or conduct or participate in the editing or management of, any newspaper or other periodical publication or electronic media... A Government servant publishing a book or participating in a public media shall at all times make it clear that the views expressed by him are his own and not that of Government.
questions.question: If a Government servant publishes a book in their personal capacity, what does Rule 8 require them to make clear?
options: That the book has been approved by the Cabinet Secretariat
That the views expressed are the officer's own and not those of the Government
That the book may not be sold for profit under any circumstances
Nothing; Rule 8 does not apply to personally authored books at all
questions.explanation: Rule 8 requires that a Government servant publishing a book or participating in public media always make clear that the views are personal, not the Government's -- it does not require Cabinet Secretariat approval of book content, impose a no-profit condition, or exempt personally authored books from the rule.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 9 -- Criticism of Government
questions.source_excerpt: No Government servant shall... make any statement of fact or opinion (i) which has the effect of an adverse criticism of any current or recent policy or action of the Central Government or a State Government... Provided that nothing in this rule shall apply to any statements made or views expressed by a Government servant in his official capacity or in the due performance of the duties assigned to him.
questions.question: A civil servant is required, as part of their official duties, to present an internal analysis to their Ministry that is critical of a recently adopted policy's implementation. Does Rule 9 prohibit this?
options: Yes, because Rule 9 bans all adverse criticism of government policy by any Government servant under any circumstances
No, because Rule 9's proviso exempts statements made in official capacity or in due performance of assigned duties, which this internal analysis is
Yes, but only if the analysis is published in a newspaper
No, but only because the officer holds a Class I post
questions.explanation: Rule 9 targets public, unofficial adverse criticism -- radio broadcasts, publications, press communications, public utterances -- and its proviso explicitly exempts statements made in official capacity or in due performance of assigned duties, which covers an internally required critical analysis; the rule is not an absolute ban, is not conditioned on newspaper publication, and the exemption is not limited to Class I posts.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 13 -- Gifts
questions.source_excerpt: On occasions such as weddings, anniversaries, funerals or religious functions... a Government servant may accept gifts from his near relatives or from his personal friends having no official dealings with him, but shall make a report to the Government, if the value of such gift exceeds -- (i) rupees twenty five thousand in the case of a Government servant holding any Group 'A' post...
questions.question: A Group 'A' officer receives a wedding gift worth Rs 30,000 from a personal friend who has no official dealings with them. What does Rule 13 require?
options: The gift must be refused outright, since any amount above zero is prohibited
The officer may accept the gift but must report it to the Government, since its value exceeds the Rs 25,000 threshold prescribed for Group 'A' officers on such occasions
The officer must donate the gift to a government charity within a week
No action is needed since wedding gifts are entirely exempt from Rule 13 regardless of value
questions.explanation: For a Group 'A' officer, Rule 13 sets Rs 25,000 as the threshold above which an occasion-based gift from a friend with no official dealings must be reported to Government -- a Rs 30,000 gift may still be accepted, but must be reported; it need not be refused outright, donated to charity, or treated as fully exempt regardless of value.

questions.locator: CCS Conduct Rules, Rule 15 -- Private trade or employment
questions.source_excerpt: (2) A Government servant may, without the previous sanction of the Government -- (a) undertake honorary work of a social or charitable nature, or (b) undertake occasional work of a literary, artistic or scientific character, or (c) participate in sports activities as an amateur...
questions.question: Which of the following activities does Rule 15 explicitly allow a Government servant to undertake WITHOUT prior Government sanction?
options: Engaging directly in a private trade or business for profit
Undertaking honorary social or charitable work, occasional literary/artistic/scientific work, or amateur sports participation
